meta.title: DBA 01 · Identity: Draw. Break. Attack.
meta.notes:
We invite pressure with control, find the player beyond it, and attack before the opponent can recover. We defend the centre together and choose our pressing height to suit the game.

Our working rule, phase by phase
- Build: keep the ball long enough to draw a press. Use the goalkeeper, centre-backs and midfielders to create a free passer.
- Progress: find a receiver between lines, carry into a gap, or pass behind a high defence. Accelerate when a line is beaten.
- Attack: keep depth through the striker; connect inside; provide width through different roles on each flank.
- Defend: use a compact 4-4-2 / 4-4-1-1 reference. Press together when the situation supports it; drop together when it does not.

Season evidence: press attraction was an established principle. An early-season 4-2-3-1 became 3-2-5 with the left-back high and the right-back tucked in.

Scope: an independent reconstruction of public match evidence. Diagrams are teaching frames, not tracked match coordinates. Positions show relationships; reproduce the identity by making similar decisions under similar pressure.

meta.title: DBA 02 · Eleven connected roles
meta.notes:
Role numbers describe jobs. They do not prescribe squad numbers or a fixed starting XI.

What each player must do well
- GK: receive under pressure; accurate short and long distribution; judge when to leave goal.
- LCB / RCB: pass through lines; defend channels; communicate early.
- LB: repeated forward and recovery runs; combinations; accurate delivery.
- RB: defend inside and outside; receive facing play; choose when to advance.
- 6: scan; receive on an angle; screen passes and win second balls.
- 8: see forward passes early; disguise direction; manage pressure.
- LW: receive under contact; turn or set quickly; recover into midfield.
- RW: win wide duels; make diagonal runs; track the opposing fullback.
- 10: receive between lines; carry at defenders; judge pass versus run.
- 9: time runs from onside; protect the ball; finish; curve pressing runs.

The midfield is adjustable: the 6 and 8 are a partnership, not two players ordered to drop onto the centre-backs every time. Keep different receiving angles and preserve a connection to the next line.

Season evidence: one documented variation used two defensive midfielders with a passing specialist higher at No. 10 and a carrier entering from the left. The jobs can be reassigned without losing the team's purpose.

boards.name: DBA 03 · First phase: Invite, then escape

meta.title: DBA 03 · First phase: Invite, then escape
meta.notes:
The slow pass has a purpose: make an opponent leave a useful defensive position.

01 Create the next pass: the goalkeeper has a return option. The centre-backs split; the midfield pair find separate lanes. A player behind a marker changes angle before calling for the ball.
02 Read the pressing jump: as the opponent moves towards a centre-back, check the pass into midfield and the space behind the presser. A calm pause is useful only while the next action remains available.
03 Connect beyond pressure: the forward receiver shows late and on a different line. If he cannot turn, he sets the ball to a facing teammate. The striker starts a depth run as the passer gains a view.
04 Choose the quickest safe exit: play through, around or over the press. A controlled long pass is part of the model. Prepare support underneath its landing point.

What we see, what we do
- The opponent does not press: carry forward; bring the team with the ball. Do not stay deep waiting for a press that never comes.
- The central receiver is tightly followed: use a set pass, move the marker, or pass directly to the next line. Do not force a turn.
- Every short option is matched: find the striker or a channel beyond the press. The 10 and nearest winger prepare for the second ball.
- The ball is trapped by the touchline: use the inside support or goalkeeper early. Reset while an exit is still available.

Coaching call: "Draw one. Find one." Short passing is a preference; progressing into a favourable situation is the objective.

boards.name: DBA 04 · Middle third A: Receive, turn, release

meta.title: DBA 04 · Middle third A: Receive, turn, release
meta.notes:
A player receiving between lines needs an action beyond the reception.

The receiver can face forward: LCB to 6, then 6 to 10. The 10 checks his shoulder, receives beyond a midfielder and plays the striker into the channel. If a defender stays deep, the 10 can carry towards him first.

A defender steps out: the player he leaves must threaten the space behind. If 9 comes short and a centre-back follows, 10 or a winger runs beyond. Someone always supplies depth.

Release cue: the passer can see forward; the runner is onside; the lane is open. Pass into the runner's path early enough to preserve the advantage. A run still has value if it moves a defender for someone else.

Season evidence: late-season attacks included direct passes from deeper midfield and the No. 10 into runs behind high defensive lines. Numbered sequences are practice examples, not fixed match scripts.

boards.name: DBA 05 · Middle third B: Set, then find the run

meta.title: DBA 05 · Middle third B: Set, then find the run
meta.notes:
The receiver has pressure behind: LCB finds 10; 10 sets to 8, who is facing forward. The striker runs beyond the defence as the set pass travels. The 10 then supports the attack instead of standing where he received.

The centre stays closed: use the wide player or change side through the midfield pair. Once the opponent shifts, look inside again. The aim is a useful advantage, not a quota of central passes.

Release cue: the passer can see forward; the runner is onside; the lane is open. Pass into the runner's path early enough to preserve the advantage.

Calls: SET (pressure is behind the receiver; return the ball to a facing teammate and move again). BEHIND (the defence is high and the passer has time; run from onside into a reachable channel).

boards.name: DBA 06 · Flanks: different sides, shared purpose

meta.title: DBA 06 · Flanks: different sides, shared purpose
meta.notes:
Our fullbacks do not automatically swap jobs whenever the ball changes side.

Left-side connections: LB provides width; LW offers an inside option; 6 or 8 supports underneath. The striker threatens the near channel. The 10 stays available between lines and RW keeps the far-side threat.

Right-side connections: RW can receive wide with 10 inside and RB below. LB can remain the far-side width. A right-back overlap is an agreed change, with the left-back or a midfielder providing the missing cover.

When delivery becomes possible
- Near channel / front of goal: 9 attacks a useful gap across the defender; do not stand next to the goalkeeper waiting for a cross.
- Cutback area: 10 or the near inside attacker arrives behind the first run. Avoid both occupying the same lane.
- Far side: the far winger attacks beyond the far defender when the delivery is likely. The far width player adjusts to avoid crowding him.
- Behind the attack: one midfielder supports the second ball while the other protects the centre; the covering defenders remain connected.

These are arrival roles, not orders to fill every position at once. Cross when a teammate has a useful advantage; combine or recycle if the box is set against us.

meta.title: DBA 07 · Transitions: attack with cover
meta.notes:
Players behind the ball determine whether we can sustain an attack or must recover.

01 Before the loss: the covering back three guard the centre and channels. The midfield pair stay connected to the ball and opposing outlets. Three plus two is a useful reference in this attacking shape, not a guarantee of safety.
02 Close enough to win it? The nearest player pressures the ball. The next player closes the easy forward pass. Others squeeze behind them only while the group can affect the opponent's next action.
03 The opponent has escaped? Delay and protect the route to goal. Recover inside first, then match the wide run. The advanced fullback returns; the remaining defenders slide across without all chasing the ball.
04 Win it back: check forward immediately. Find 9, 10 or a runner if the opponent is open. If the receiver is trapped, secure the first pass and restore the shape.

The key decision: can we pressure the ball before the opponent can play forward? If yes, support the challenge together. If no, recover together. One isolated press can remove the player who should have protected the centre.

Three checks before an extra player joins: who covers the channel? Who blocks the first pass into their striker? Who is available if our attack needs to restart? If these jobs are vacant, keep the extra player underneath.

Season evidence: transition defence was a real weakness in part of the season. An early-December review also recorded a deeper line than the previous season and less effective offside control. Recovery decisions are essential work.

boards.name: DBA 08 · Defending: close the centre together

meta.title: DBA 08 · Defending: close the centre together
meta.notes:
The front two, midfield four and back four must respond to the same ball movement. Our team attacks to the right; the opponent attacks towards our goal.

01 Front pair: 9 and 10 discourage an easy pass into the central midfielder. One engages the carrier; the other protects the central route. If 10 drops slightly, the shape reads as 4-4-1-1.
02 Wide pass: RW moves towards the receiver as the pass travels. 8 shifts across behind him. RB controls the next wide threat. The far winger narrows; he does not stay on the opposite touchline.
03 Protect the gaps: the nearest centre-back covers behind the fullback. The far defenders narrow. Midfielders track dangerous runs while keeping sight of the ball; a handover must be communicated.
04 Reset the block: if we cannot reach the ball, stop stretching towards it. Recover the distances between lines and make the opponent play around the group.

Defensive-line response
- Opponent under effective pressure or forced backwards: move up together when the pass and runner positions permit. The goalkeeper moves with the team to cover space behind.
- Opponent facing forward with time: prepare to drop and track the run. Do not step forward solely because we want to hold a high line.
- A runner is clearly offside: keep collective discipline, but continue defending until the decision is made. Never stop because a teammate appeals.
- An opponent breaks through midfield: a defender delays the carrier while others protect depth and passing lanes. Recovering midfielders must rejoin quickly.

A high line needs pressure on the pass and shared timing. Its height changes with the ball, the opponent and the match plan.

boards.name: DBA 09 · Choose the height A: higher press

meta.title: DBA 09 · Choose the height A: higher press
meta.notes:
A higher press and a deeper block belong to the same game model.

Press with the whole team: on a slow square pass, poor touch or receiver facing his own goal, 9 curves his run to limit the next pass. 10 controls the nearby central outlet. The winger and midfielder move behind the first presser; the defence comes up.

If the first pressure fails: delay the forward attack and protect depth. The players beaten by the pass recover immediately. Avoid another unsupported jump that leaves more space.

Make the decision before the match, then review it: use a higher press when the group can close the next options and defend the space behind. Use the deeper plan when protecting the box and counterattacking better suits the opponent or game state.

Calls: TOGETHER (the press is on; support the first player and close the next options). RECOVER (the opponent can play forward beyond our pressure; protect depth and rebuild the block).

Season evidence: two April knockout legs showed the contrast: a compact 4-4-2 became 5-4-1 when retreating; the return used a much higher collective press and quicker forward play. These were different match plans, not a single permanent height.

meta.title: DBA 10 · Choose the height B: deeper 5-4-1
meta.notes:
Add a defender without adding a player: 6 drops into the defensive line; 10 returns to midfield alongside 8, with the wide players outside them. The striker remains the main outlet. This is a role-based example of the rotation.

Defend the box patiently: stay close enough to cover the teammate who engages. Stop a cross when possible; protect the central finishing spaces. On a regain, find the outlet or secure a support pass.

Make the decision before the match, then review it: use the deeper plan when protecting the box and counterattacking better suits the opponent or game state.

Season evidence: a compact 4-4-2 became 5-4-1 when retreating in an April knockout leg.

meta.title: DBA 11 · Change jobs, keep connections
meta.notes:
The season contained several attacking versions. Use a clear assignment for each one.

A Asymmetric base: LB supplies the left width; LW moves inside; 10 links around 9; RW can hold the right width; RB supports the covering line. Two inside receivers ahead of the midfield pair, with different providers of width.
B Both wide players inside: LW and RW work as extra receivers between lines. 10 adjusts away from them; 9 preserves depth. Width and covering duties must be reassigned. More central combinations, but fewer immediate wide outlets unless their replacements are timed well.
C Creator higher: two defensive midfield profiles work below a passing No. 10. A left-sided carrier moves in to connect and run. More protection below the ball and passing quality closer to the striker.
D Direct depth threat: one fast striker as the primary run behind; 10 and the wide players support him. The first forward pass can come from deeper positions. More attacks into the space behind the defence, with runners close enough to support the next action.

When both wingers come inside: do not place LW, 10 and RW in one flat line. Stagger their heights and let one move away when another checks short. Send an outside player only after deciding who protects that side if the ball is lost.
When the opponent crowds the centre: use an outside receiver, switch sides or play behind the pressing line. More players in the centre does not automatically produce a free passing lane.

Our repeatable rule: every role change must preserve four jobs: an outlet underneath, a receiver beyond the press, a threat behind the defence, and cover if possession is lost. Check the relationships before naming a new formation.

The regular attacking reference is one striker with support. Two centre-forwards can be an option, but making them permanent would misrepresent the model.

boards.name: DBA 12 · Practice 1: escape pressure, 8v6 plus a target

meta.title: DBA 12 · Practice 1: escape pressure, 8v6 plus a target
meta.notes:
Area: start around 45 x 50 m with a full-size goal and a target zone beyond the press. Build with GK, back four, 6, 8 and 10 against six pressers. A separate target represents 9. Restart from GK.

Scoring: one point for a controlled pass to the target; two when the target can set to an arriving 10. Pressers score in the main goal on a regain.

Coach the trigger: let the press choose whether to jump, screen or match players. Reward the correct exit through, around or over it. Ask the receiver what he saw before the pass. Stop only to fix a missing angle or an unsupported next action.

Suggested dose: 3-4 bouts of 4 minutes, brief feedback between bouts. Choose two practices for a session, then finish with freer play. Dimensions and timings are starting points for an adult 11v11 group; adjust to age, fitness and pitch space.

Keep decisions live. Avoid blanket two-touch rules, compulsory central passes or scripted pressing every time: each removes a choice this model needs players to recognise.

meta.notes:
Area: full width and about 75-90 m long, adjusted to the players. Alternate blocks of play with a mid-block plan, a high-press plan and a deeper block. Restart from the opposition goalkeeper. Award goals normally; record whether the first press had support and whether a regain led to a useful forward action.

Coach the shared response: do not demand a press on every pass. The whole group must recognise when to go and when to reset. After a bypass, assess the delay, protection of depth and recovery runs. After a regain, assess the first decision before judging the finish.

boards.name: DBA 15 · The player card: shared calls

meta.title: DBA 15 · The player card: shared calls
meta.notes:
A small set of shared calls should carry the whole game model.

- DRAW: we have control and a safe next pass. Invite an opponent to leave his position.
- FACE: the receiver can turn. Support his forward action; start the depth run.
- SET: pressure is behind the receiver. Return the ball to a facing teammate and move again.
- BEHIND: the defence is high and the passer has time. Run from onside into a reachable channel.
- OUTSIDE: the middle is blocked. Use width, make the opponent shift, then reassess the next gap.
- TOGETHER: the press is on. Support the first player and close the next options.
- RECOVER: the opponent can play forward beyond our pressure. Protect depth and rebuild the block.

Before kick-off: agree the attacking version, which fullback supplies width, the midfield roles, the first pressing line and the outlet on a regain. Identify the opponent's free player and main run behind.

At the break: is the press being drawn? Who is free but hard to reach? Can our 10 receive facing forward? Which side is exposed on losses? Change the role causing the problem before changing every position.

Review after the match
- Progress through pressure: successful and failed exits, split into through / around / over. Note whether the next receiver had support.
- Attacking advantage: receipts between lines facing forward; useful runs behind; wide receptions with time; chances following these actions.
- Protection: losses followed by a shot or clear forward break. Identify the missing pressure, cover or recovery decision.
- Collective defending: presses that forced play back or won the ball; presses bypassed; line decisions that exposed space behind.

Use your own match baseline. These are review measures, not season statistics or performance targets.
